name: Vriddhagireeswarar Temple, Vriddhachalam (Thirumuthukundram)
deity: Shiva as Pazhamalainathar (Vriddhagireeswarar), with the goddesses Periyanayaki (Vriddhambigai) and Balambigai
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu on the Manimuktha, sung by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in the Tevaram (7th–8th century); enlarged under Sembiyan Mahadevi in the 10th century
dynasty: Chola (Sembiyan Mahadevi, reign of Uttama Chola), with later additions
summary: In the heart of Vriddhachalam, the Thirumuthukundram or 'old hill' of the Tevaram, Shiva is worshipped as Pazhamalainathar, the Lord of the ancient hill, praised by all three Tevaram saints.

sections.history: Vriddhachalam is a busy town of Cuddalore district on the banks of the Manimuktha, and its great Shiva temple is the Thirumuthukundram of the Tevaram. Both names mean the same thing — the old hill, in Tamil and in Sanskrit. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams, counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu, and it was praised by all three Tevaram saints, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar. The temple carries several Chola inscriptions, and a record of the reign of Uttama Chola, around 982 CE, tells that the queen-mother Sembiyan Mahadevi, the great temple-builder of her age, raised the central shrine and the shrines of the attendant deities. Later generations added the outer enclosures and towers that crowd the town centre today.
sections.architecture: This is a large Dravidian temple of five concentric enclosures, with the sanctum of Pazhamalainathar at its heart and separate shrines for the two goddesses, Periyanayaki, the elder, and Balambigai, the young. Among the temple's five Vinayaka shrines the best known is Aazhathu Vinayagar, the Ganesha of the depths, whose shrine lies well below the level of the surrounding court. The temple counts several sacred waters — the Manimuktha river near the northern gateway, the Nityananda well, and the Agni, Chakra and Kubera theerthams.
sections.legends: The best-loved story belongs to Sundarar. When he sang here, the Lord rewarded him with twelve thousand gold coins. Sundarar was anxious about carrying such wealth on the road, so the Lord told him to cast the gold into the Manimuktha and promised that he would receive it back from the temple tank at Tiruvarur — and, the Periya Puranam tells, so he did. Tradition also explains the Lord's name: Pazhamalai, the ancient hill, the first of all hills.
sections.festivals: The chief festival is the brahmotsavam that culminates on Masi Magam (February–March), when great crowds bathe in the Manimuktha and the deities are taken out in procession. It is one of three annual festivals, and Maha Shivaratri, Arudra Darshanam and the monthly Pradosham are also kept. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Vriddhachalam is a temple town in the true sense, its streets running up to the gopurams. Bathe or sprinkle water at the Manimuktha by the northern gate, as pilgrims have done for centuries, step down to Aazhathu Vinayagar, and worship at the shrines of both goddesses. Remember Sundarar's gold on the riverbank, and allow time for the many enclosures.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure; hours may be extended on festival days. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in the centre of Vriddhachalam, a short auto ride from the bus stand. Vriddhachalam Junction is on the main Chennai–Tiruchirappalli railway line; Tiruchirappalli and Puducherry are the nearest airports, with Chennai about 200 km away by road.
